passage: My sister Disha is ten and very serious about rules, so I was surprised last week. Her friend Rekha invited her home for Christmas Eve, and Disha came back talking nonstop. She told me Rekha's family sang songs in the evening and put a small star on top of the tree. She had asked Rekha's mother why they made a little crib with animals, and listened to the whole answer. At dinner, Mummy asked if she ate the cake. "Only after I asked if it had egg," Disha said. "Aunty didn't mind. She made me a plain one." Then Disha tied a paper star to our window. I don't know exactly what she felt, but she hummed while she did it. 🙂

qa.q: What did Disha tie to the window after the visit?
qa.a: She tied a paper star to the family's window.

qa.q: What does Disha's nonstop talk and humming suggest she felt about Rekha's festival?
qa.a: She came back talking nonstop, listened to the full answer about the crib, and hummed while hanging a paper star, which suggests curiosity and admiration.

qa.q: What was respectful about how Disha handled the cake?
qa.a: She asked politely about egg instead of refusing or eating it without thinking, which respected both her own family's food habits and her host's effort.

qa.q: How might Rekha's mother see Disha after the evening?
qa.a: She probably saw a curious, polite guest who took an interest in their customs, and was happy to make a plain cake so Disha could join in.

grounding: It shows, through a sibling's eyes, a child learning about a friend's faith festival and respecting it while keeping her own practices.

passage:
Monday: Rukmini told the class that her neighbours were fasting through the day for Ramzan and she sometimes joined their evening meal, and Rashmi snorted, "No lunch for a month? That's silly." Rukmini went quiet. Rashmi saw her face and felt a bit bad, but didn't say anything.

Thursday: Rashmi asked her mother about it. Amma explained that Rashmi's Nani also fasted on some days, in her own way, and that it meant something to her. Rashmi thought about that a long time.

The next Tuesday: Rukmini brought dates that her neighbour had sent for the evening meal. Rashmi took one, said, "Thank you, and sorry about Monday," and asked what they ate first when the fast ended.

qa.q: What did Rukmini bring to school on the next Tuesday?
qa.a: She brought dates her neighbour had sent for the evening meal.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she saw Rukmini go quiet on Monday?
qa.a: She felt a bit bad because she realised her snort had hurt Rukmini, though she wasn't ready to say so yet.

qa.q: What helped Rashmi change her attitude, and what could she try next?
qa.a: Linking the fast to her own Nani's fasting helped her see its meaning; next time she could ask a question first instead of laughing.

qa.q: What is it like for Rukmini when Rashmi apologises and asks about the meal?
qa.a: It probably feels like relief and being taken seriously, since the practice she shared is now treated with interest instead of mockery.

grounding: It shows a child moving over several days from mocking a different faith practice to asking about it respectfully.

passage: Sit, Swati, I'll tell you about Manjula, my best friend when I was your age. Our lane had a small gurdwara at one end. Every Sunday we could smell the dal from the langar kitchen. Manjula was curious, but her father said, "That's their place, not ours." One day she walked in with her head uncovered, and a lady gently handed her a scarf. Manjula went red. The lady just smiled and showed her where to wash her hands. After that, Manjula helped roll rotis there every week, and she still lit her diya at home every evening. When I asked if she had changed religions, she laughed. "No, silly. I just learned their rules so I don't hurt anyone."

qa.q: What did the lady hand Manjula when she walked in?
qa.a: She gently handed her a scarf to cover her head.

qa.q: Why did Manjula go red when the lady handed her the scarf?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed because she realised she had broken a custom of the place without knowing, and she worried she might have been disrespectful.

qa.q: What could Swati take from Manjula's story if she visits another faith's place?
qa.a: She could ask or watch for the customs, like covering her head or washing hands, and follow them while still keeping her own practices at home.

qa.q: How might Manjula's father have seen her weekly visits?
qa.a: He may have worried at first that she was crossing a line, but he might see over time that she kept her own diya and simply learned to respect her neighbours.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood friend learning the customs of another faith's place of worship and respecting them while keeping her own.

passage: Indu's eleventh birthday party was at seven, and she had invited her whole class, but the evening went wrong the moment Payal said on the phone, 'Sorry, I can't eat after sunset. It's Paryushan. My family is fasting this week.' Indu stared at the cake box. 'But the cake!' She almost said, 'Just once won't matter.' Then she remembered how much Payal knew about Christmas, and how she'd asked about the crib in Indu's house without laughing. There was only an hour before sunset. Indu ran to Mamma. 'Can we cut the cake early, at six, for anyone who comes?' Mamma nodded. Payal came at six, grinning, and ate first. 'You changed it for me?' 'Obviously.'

qa.q: Why couldn't Payal eat at the party at seven?
qa.a: It was Paryushan and her family was fasting, so she couldn't eat after sunset.

qa.q: Why did Indu stop herself from saying 'Just once won't matter'?
qa.a: She remembered how respectfully Payal had asked about Christmas and the crib, and wanted to show the same respect back.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Moving the cake cutting before sunset kept Payal included without asking her to break her family's practice.

qa.q: How might Payal have felt when she learned Indu changed the time?
qa.a: She would likely feel respected and cared for, and happy she could fully join the birthday. 🙏

grounding: Shows a child respecting a friend's faith practice under time pressure.

passage: Kamal had never been to a Ganesh pandal before. His classmate Rukmini's colony in Andheri had set one up under a tent of marigolds, and she'd dragged him along after school. The drums were so loud his chest buzzed. He stood near the back, unsure. Could he go in? Should he take off his sneakers? He watched others leave their shoes at the side and did the same. 'Why does Ganpati have a mouse?' he whispered. Rukmini explained, and he listened carefully. Aunties were making rangoli, and one handed him the orange powder. He drew a careful star. On the way home, he asked Rukmini, 'Will you come to our house for Eid? Ammi makes sheer khurma.' 'Obviously!'

qa.q: What did Kamal draw with the orange powder?
qa.a: He drew a careful star in the rangoli.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling as he stood near the back of the pandal?
qa.a: He felt unsure and a bit nervous, not knowing the customs and not wanting to do something wrong.

qa.q: How did Kamal show respect at a festival that wasn't his own?
qa.a: He watched how others behaved, followed along, asked questions quietly and joined in with the rangoli.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see Kamal's invitation to Eid?
qa.a: She would likely feel happy that sharing her festival led to him wanting to share his.

grounding: Shows a child learning about and respecting a friend's festival different from his own.

passage:
“Noor, can I really come to your Iftar?”
“Of course, Pallavi. Ammi said bring your appetite.”
“But you've been fasting all day. Aren't you starving?”
“A bit. But it's special. We fast in Ramzan to remember people who are hungry and to be close to God.”
“Do I have to do anything special?”
“Just wait till the call to prayer. Then we break the fast with dates.”
At Noor's house, Pallavi sat quietly as the family prayed. When the call came, Noor handed her a date. “Now.”
Pallavi ate it. “Thank you for letting me come.”
Noor grinned. “Next Diwali, I'm coming to yours for sweets.”

qa.q: What does Noor's family break the fast with?
qa.a: They break the fast with dates.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel about being invited to Iftar?
qa.a: She felt excited and curious, but a little unsure what to do.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do that showed respect?
qa.a: She asked what to do, sat quietly during prayer and thanked Noor's family.

qa.q: How might Noor feel when Pallavi joins her family's Iftar?
qa.a: She probably feels happy and proud to share her tradition with her friend.

grounding: A ten-year-old learns respectfully about her friend's Ramzan fast and Iftar.

passage:
Last year, I stayed over at my friend Irawati's house during Paryushan. I'm Swati. I didn't know much about it except that her family is Jain.
At dinner, they ate before sunset, and the food had no onion, garlic or root vegetables. I asked why, and Irawati's grandmother explained that they try not to harm even tiny living things during these days.
I felt a little embarrassed that I had brought potato chips as a gift. Irawati laughed and said we'd eat them another day.
That night, I watched her family sit quietly for their prayers. I didn't join in, but I didn't talk either. It felt peaceful.

qa.q: What did Irawati's family not eat during Paryushan?
qa.a: Onion, garlic or root vegetables.

qa.q: How did Swati feel about the gift of potato chips?
qa.a: Swati felt a little embarrassed, realising it didn't fit the family's practice.

qa.q: What did Swati do that showed respect?
qa.a: Swati asked politely, listened to the explanation and stayed quiet during the prayers.

qa.q: How did Irawati react to the chips?
qa.a: She laughed kindly and said they'd eat them another day.

grounding: A student learns about and respects a friend's Jain festival practices.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 6. Sunaina Das.
Before Gurpurab, Harpreet told the class about langar, the free kitchen at her gurdwara, where anyone can eat, sitting on the floor together.
Bhupen (eleven) asked many questions: “Can anyone come? Even if they're not Sikh? Why cover the head?” Harpreet answered each one.
On Sunday, Bhupen went with Harpreet's family to the gurdwara, covered his head with a scarf, and helped serve rotis. He told the class on Monday, “Everybody ate together. Nobody asked who I was.”
Next step: I'll invite families to share one festival each month.

qa.q: What did Bhupen help serve at the gurdwara?
qa.a: He helped serve rotis.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel about the langar after visiting?
qa.a: He felt moved and impressed that everyone ate together without being asked who they were.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do that showed respect for Harpreet's faith?
qa.a: He asked respectful questions, covered his head and helped serve.

qa.q: How might Harpreet feel when Bhupen comes to the gurdwara?
qa.a: She probably feels proud and happy that he wanted to learn about her faith.

grounding: A teacher notes an eleven-year-old learning about and respecting a classmate's Sikh practice.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today I had lunch at Harsha's home. His family is Jain. It's Paryushan, so they don't eat after sunset, and no onion or garlic.
His mother gave us dal and roti without onions. I thought it'd be bland. It wasn't!
Then Harsha said they'd been fasting for part of the week. I asked if it was hard. He said, "Sometimes. It's about slowing down and thinking."
I had a chocolate in my bag. I didn't eat it there. It felt wrong.
On the way home, I thought about how our family eats whatever. His family thinks about every bite.
— Mohit

qa.q: What festival period was it for Harsha's family?
qa.a: Paryushan.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when he didn't eat the chocolate?
qa.a: Mohit felt respectful and a bit awkward, not wanting to eat it in front of fasting people.

qa.q: How could Mohit keep showing respect for Harsha's family's practices?
qa.a: Mohit can keep asking kindly, eat what's offered, and remember their fasting times when inviting Harsha out.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel when Mohit asks about fasting?
qa.a: Harsha probably feels respected that Mohit wanted to understand, not laugh.

grounding: A child writes about learning and respecting a friend's Jain festival practices.

passage:
The drums of Durga Puja were beating across the village. Bidisha tugged Parveen's hand. "Come see our pandal!"
Parveen hesitated at the entrance. She'd never been inside one.
"You don't have to pray," said Bidisha. "Just look."
Inside, the goddess had ten arms. Parveen stared at the lion and the colours. Bidisha's grandmother offered her prasad. Parveen looked at Bidisha, unsure.
"You can take it or not," Bidisha whispered. "Both are fine."
Parveen took it with both hands, like Bidisha did. "Thank you, Dida."
Later, Parveen said, "Come to our home on Eid. Ammi makes sevai."

qa.q: How many arms did the goddess have?
qa.a: Ten arms.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when she hesitated at the entrance?
qa.a: Parveen felt unsure and a little nervous, never having been inside a pandal.

qa.q: What did Bidisha say that made it easier for Parveen?
qa.a: She said Parveen didn't have to pray and could take prasad or not, which respected Parveen's own faith.

qa.q: How might Bidisha's grandmother see Parveen taking prasad with both hands?
qa.a: Bidisha's grandmother likely feels touched and respected by Parveen's polite gesture.

grounding: Two village children of different faiths visit a Durga Puja pandal with respect.

passage:
It was Ramadan, and Hiroshi noticed Jamal wasn't eating lunch at their school in Tokyo.
"Are you sick?"
"No, I'm fasting. No food or water from sunrise to sunset. It's Ramadan."
"Not even water? Isn't that hard?"
"Sometimes. It helps me remember people who don't have enough."
Hiroshi looked at his onigiri. He quietly put it back in his bag and ate it later in the corridor.
The next week, Jamal's family invited him to iftar. Hiroshi brought a box of dates his mother bought. He watched Jamal's family pray, then eat together, laughing.
"Thank you for coming," said Jamal.

qa.q: What does Jamal say he doesn't have from sunrise to sunset?
qa.a: No food or water.

qa.q: What was Hiroshi feeling when he put his onigiri back?
qa.a: Hiroshi felt considerate and a little awkward about eating in front of Jamal.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi do that showed respect?
qa.a: He asked kindly, ate away from Jamal, and came to iftar with a thoughtful gift.

qa.q: How might Jamal feel when Hiroshi comes to iftar?
qa.a: Jamal is likely happy and grateful 😊 that his friend wanted to share his tradition.

grounding: A child in Japan learns about and respects his friend's Ramadan fast.

passage:
In the school lunch room, Sumit opened his tiffin: plain roti and moong, no onion, no garlic. Two boys at the table sniffed.
"Again boring food?"
"It's Paryushan," Sumit said. "We don't eat root vegetables for these days."
"Why? Potatoes don't have feelings," one boy laughed.
Sachin, who had been about to laugh too, stopped. He actually wanted to know. "Wait, why root vegetables?"
Sumit explained that pulling them up kills the whole plant and lots of tiny life in the soil, and his family tries to harm less during these days.
Sachin thought about it. "That's kind of big." Next day he left the potato sabzi out of his tiffin when he sat with Sumit, just to see how it felt.

qa.q: What was in Sumit's tiffin?
qa.a: Plain roti and moong, no onion, no garlic.

qa.q: Why did Sachin stop himself from laughing?
qa.a: Sachin felt curious and wanted to understand, and the joke suddenly seemed unkind next to Sumit's reason.

qa.q: How could a teacher help the lunch table understand Sumit's practice?
qa.a: A teacher could invite students to share their festival or food customs, so differences are explained and not mocked.

qa.q: What is it like for Sumit when his food is called boring every day?
qa.a: It may feel tiring and hurtful for Sumit, having to defend his faith over lunch instead of just eating.

grounding: Illustrates a child choosing to learn about and respect a classmate's religious practice instead of mocking it.

passage:
I'm Tanuja. I'll tell you what I saw on Christmas Eve in our colony.
Mrs D'Costa had set up a crib under the stairs, with clay figures and cotton for snow. Most of us just grabbed the plum cake and ran. Neelam didn't. She crouched and asked what each figure was, even the donkey. Mrs D'Costa explained the shepherds and the star. Neelam kept nodding.
When the carollers stopped for a prayer, some kids kept talking. Neelam put her finger to her lips and stood still with her hands folded, though her family goes to the temple, not church.
Afterwards Mrs D'Costa gave her an extra slice. I don't know exactly what Neelam was thinking. She looked like someone who'd been let into a secret.

qa.q: What did Mrs D'Costa use for snow in the crib?
qa.a: She used cotton for snow.

qa.q: What does Neelam's expression afterwards suggest, according to Tanuja?
qa.a: Neelam seemed delighted and moved, like someone who'd been let into a secret, though Tanuja can't be sure.

qa.q: What would you advise the kids who kept talking during the prayer?
qa.a: Even if it isn't your own faith, stay quiet for a few moments; it shows respect and costs nothing.

qa.q: How might Mrs D'Costa have felt about Neelam's questions?
qa.a: Mrs D'Costa probably felt touched and valued, since someone from another faith cared enough to ask about her festival.

grounding: Shows, through a neighbour's eyes, a child learning about and respecting a festival of another faith.

passage:
Monday, the week of Navroz. Ira said the fire temple was "weird" because she wasn't allowed inside. Zubin went quiet and didn't share his chips at break.
Wednesday. Ira asked him why he was sulking. Zubin said, "It's not weird. It's just ours." He explained that the fire has been kept burning for years and years, and only Parsis go in. Ira said, "That's not fair to me." Zubin shrugged: "Your family's puja room isn't for everyone either."
Ira thought about that all afternoon.
Saturday. Zubin's mother invited her for Navroz lunch. Ira sat outside the temple gate while they prayed, then ate sali boti and falooda at their table. "Thanks for waiting," Zubin said. She said, "It's your place. I get it now."

qa.q: What did Ira eat at Zubin's Navroz lunch?
qa.a: Ira ate sali boti and falooda.

qa.q: Why did Zubin go quiet and not share his chips on Monday?
qa.a: Zubin felt hurt and offended that Ira called his fire temple weird.

qa.q: Which comparison helped Ira understand, and why?
qa.a: Zubin compared the temple to her family's puja room, which let her see the rule from her own experience.

qa.q: How might Zubin's mother see Ira waiting at the gate?
qa.a: His mother might feel respected and warm towards Ira, seeing she honoured their custom instead of complaining.

grounding: Illustrates a child, over several days, moving from calling another faith's practice weird to respecting it.

passage:
Jatin, you asked why I go to the Christmas service at St. Mary's every year when we're Hindu. Let me tell you.
When I was nine, my best friend was Thomas from the next house. One December he invited me to the midnight service. I told my father, "Won't God be angry if I go?"
My father said, "Go and watch with respect. Don't mock anything. Stand when they stand."
The church was full of candles and a song I didn't know. I was nervous, but Thomas's grandmother gave me a plum cake and said, "Welcome, son."
Next Diwali, Thomas lit lamps with us on our roof. We did that for sixty years, until he passed.
So this year, will you come with me?

qa.q: What did Thomas's grandmother give the young storyteller?
qa.a: She gave him a plum cake.

qa.q: What was the young storyteller feeling inside the church?
qa.a: He felt nervous in a new place with unfamiliar songs, but also welcomed when Thomas's grandmother greeted him.

qa.q: What choice inside the story set the friendship on a good path?
qa.a: The father's advice to go and watch with respect, standing when others stood, let the boy join without offending anyone.

qa.q: How might Thomas have felt when his friend came to the service?
qa.a: Thomas probably felt happy and valued, seeing his best friend honour his festival, which he returned by lighting Diwali lamps.

grounding: Shows an elder passing on a lifelong habit of respecting and joining in another faith's festival.
